choices: You, because you were the first provider on scene
The AEMT, because the paramedic's hands will be busy intubating
The paramedic, because she is the highest-level provider on scene
The medical control physician at the hospital
questions.explanation: The highest-level provider on scene serves as team leader and directs the team's work, even while performing a procedure herself.
questions.question: You were first on scene with an unresponsive woman who isn't breathing, and you've been ventilating her with a bag-mask device. An ALS crew arrives: the paramedic starts preparing to intubate while her AEMT partner works on an IV. Who should direct the team's work from this point on?

choices: Take over as team leader so the paramedic can concentrate
Assist the paramedic with the intubation
Assist the AEMT with the IV line
Ask the team leader which role she needs you to fill
questions.explanation: After the handoff, roles come from the team leader. Asking what she needs keeps the team coordinated instead of duplicating work someone is already doing.
questions.question: You've just given your verbal report to the paramedic. She is setting up to intubate and the AEMT is starting an IV, so both of their hands are full. What's the best way to make yourself useful now?

choices: Over the radio, before the ambulance arrives
Face to face, inside the house
Face to face, outside the house once the patient is loaded
Over the radio, after the ambulance leaves for the hospital
questions.explanation: The report goes directly to the crew taking over, face to face at the patient's side, so information and care transfer together without delay.
questions.question: You're ventilating an unresponsive woman with a bag-mask device when the ALS crew walks into the house. They need your findings before they take over her care. When and how should you give your verbal report?

choices: The team leader
The AEMT
The physician at the emergency department
The patient's family
questions.explanation: Relevant patient information goes to the team leader, who is coordinating care and making sure nothing important gets missed.
questions.question: While the paramedic and AEMT work on the patient, you search the house and find her medication list and medical history paperwork. Who should you give this information to?

choices: Only his most recent vital signs, since the earlier findings no longer matter
A list of every patient currently being treated in the tent
How he presented on your first assessment with his vital signs, the treatments given so far, and his current status
Your recommendation for which hospital should receive him
questions.explanation: A complete handoff covers the patient's initial presentation and vital signs, everything that has been done for him, and where he stands now.
questions.question: At a 10K race medical tent, a transport crew arrives for your heatstroke patient. The paramedic who has been directing his care is tied up with another patient, so you give the report. What should it include?

choices: It lets the original crew clear the scene sooner
Care isn't interrupted, and a respectful face-to-face exchange in a common, standardized format — with a chance for questions or a summary back — keeps the information accurate
It removes the need for any written documentation afterward
It keeps the patient from hearing what is said about his condition
questions.explanation: Transfers of care should happen with as little interruption to treatment as possible, using good eye contact, a common language or standardized format, and questions or a read-back to catch misunderstandings.
questions.question: You give your report to the arriving ALS crew while the paramedic keeps treating the patient, instead of everyone stopping to talk. Beyond keeping care moving, what makes a transfer like this work well?

choices: Assemble the intubation equipment she'll need
Hold the patient's head steady for the tube placement
Get ready to monitor the patient once the tube is in
Keep ventilating the patient with the bag-mask device
questions.explanation: The patient isn't breathing on her own, so ventilation can't pause while equipment is prepared. Preparing the patient — by continuing to ventilate — comes first.
questions.question: The paramedic asks you to assist her with intubating the apneic patient. She's still getting her equipment ready. What should you do first?

choices: Raise the patient's legs
Lift the patient's neck
Pad under the patient's shoulders
Turn the patient onto her side
questions.explanation: Padding under the shoulders helps align the airway so the paramedic can see what she needs to place the tube.
questions.question: The paramedic asks you to help position the patient to make intubation easier. Which action best helps her visualize the airway?

choices: Nothing — more resistance is expected once a patient is intubated
Alert the team leader right away that the bag is offering more resistance
Slow your ventilation rate until the resistance eases
Pull the tube and go back to the oral airway
questions.explanation: A change in bag resistance can signal an airway or tube problem. The team leader needs to hear about it immediately, not after it becomes a crisis.
questions.question: You're ventilating the patient through the newly placed ET tube when the bag suddenly offers noticeably more resistance than it did a minute ago. What should you do?

choices: Whether the fluid is flowing, and the insertion site for swelling, bleeding, leaking, or discoloration
The patient's temperature every five minutes
Whether the paramedic remembered to chart the IV start time
The oxygen saturation trend and nothing else
questions.explanation: A kinked or blocked tube, an empty bag, or an infiltrating site all show up in the flow or at the insertion point. Watch for them and report abnormal findings to the paramedic.
questions.question: You set up the IV for the paramedic in the medical tent — spiking the bag, filling the drip chamber, and clearing all the air from the tubing. Once the line is running, what should you keep an eye on?

choices: Immediately inform the team leader that the AEMT needs help
Call the AEMT's supervisor
Don't engage in the moment; calmly speak with the AEMT about the situation after the call
Take the IV supplies and start the line yourself
questions.explanation: Arguing at the patient's side helps no one. With the patient stable, let the moment pass and address the teamwork problem calmly with the AEMT after the call.
questions.question: You offer to help the AEMT, who is clearly struggling to establish the IV line. He tells you flatly that he doesn't need any help. The patient is stable and being cared for. What's the best response?

choices: Stay out of it until the two of them settle the disagreement
Finish packaging first, then mention the ventilation problem
Document the disagreement so it can be reviewed later
Speak up and make sure ventilation gets back on track, even if that means taking over the bag yourself
questions.explanation: When a team breakdown disrupts critical patient care, immediate intervention is required — draw the paramedic's attention to the inadequate ventilation or take over ventilations yourself so care continues while they resolve the issue.
questions.question: As the crew starts packaging the patient, the paramedic and AEMT get into a disagreement about how to do it — and you notice the patient is no longer being ventilated at the appropriate rate. How should you proceed?

choices: Train and practice together frequently and realistically
Exchange phone numbers so you can text during calls
Let the highest-ranking provider handle all communication
Review each other's patient care reports after every call
questions.explanation: Preparation and training are the keys to team performance. Providers of all levels who train together regularly learn to work as a true team instead of independent providers.
questions.question: You and the ALS crew you frequently respond with function more like strangers than a team — people work in parallel and communication is clumsy. What would most improve how you perform together on future calls?

choices: A diabetic emergency and a fractured hip
A heat-related problem, along with something like an ankle sprain, a muscle pull, or blisters
Hypothermia and frostbite
An allergic reaction to something he ate before the race
questions.explanation: The limp points to a leg or foot problem — a sprain, muscle pull, or blisters. Flushed skin and confusion in extreme heat and humidity point to a heat-related illness.
questions.question: It's 95°F and very humid at a 10K race. A runner limps into the medical tent; he's flushed and seems a bit confused. Given how he presents and the conditions out on the course, which problems should you most expect to find?
questions.topic: Recognizing and escalating a deteriorating patient

choices: A full set of vital signs, including a temperature
His blood glucose and nothing else
A detailed history of his training routine
Whether he feels well enough to finish the race
questions.explanation: With the ABCs stable, vital signs — including a temperature in these conditions — are what tell you how serious his condition is.
questions.question: Your new tent patient is flushed and confused. You've confirmed his airway, breathing, and circulation are stable. What should you assess next to figure out what's going on with him?
questions.topic: Recognizing and escalating a deteriorating patient

choices: Keep observing him quietly so you don't disturb the others
Give him some oral fluids and recheck him in 15 minutes
Move him to a cot in the shade and let him rest
Notify the paramedic or physician assistant immediately, maintain his airway, and start cooling measures while you wait
questions.explanation: His instability is beyond your level of care. Alert a higher-level provider right away while you protect his airway and begin cooling — those two jobs can't wait.
questions.question: Your tent patient's vitals are: respirations 28, pulse 124 and a bit thready, blood pressure 94/60, temperature 104°F. He suddenly vomits and becomes even more confused. A paramedic and a physician assistant are in the tent treating other patients. What should you do now?
questions.topic: Recognizing and escalating a deteriorating patient

choices: He has recovered enough to be released from the tent
He is likely in compensated shock from dehydration and possible heatstroke — slightly improved, but still seriously ill
His condition has clearly worsened since the first set of vitals
These are normal numbers for a man who just ran a race
questions.explanation: Rates and pressure have improved slightly, but a pulse of 116, a borderline pressure, and persistent confusion mean compensated shock. He is still a seriously ill patient.
questions.question: After cooling measures and about half a liter of IV fluid, you repeat the vitals on your heat patient: respirations 20, pulse 116, blood pressure 98/62. He is still very confused. How do these numbers read?
questions.topic: Recognizing and escalating a deteriorating patient

choices: The continuum of care — connected, consistent care from first contact to discharge, with each provider sharing information and building on the last one's work
A group of providers each working independently
Why BLS providers should avoid getting ALS involved
That the hospital is responsible for all field decisions
questions.explanation: The continuum of care is consistent patient care across the whole team, from first contact to discharge. Good communication at each step improves team performance, safety, and the patient's outcome.
questions.question: Follow Robert's care through the tent: you assessed him and reported your findings to the paramedic, assisted with his treatment, then briefed the ALS transport crew, who will hand him off to the hospital staff. When a chain like this works well, what does it demonstrate?

choices: Community paramedicine
Crew resource management
Mobile integrated health care
Continuum of care
questions.explanation: Mobile integrated health care is a method of delivering health care within the community rather than at a physician's office or hospital.
questions.question: A health system decides to bring care to patients where they live — sending providers out into homes and neighborhoods instead of requiring every visit to happen at a physician's office or a hospital. This model of delivering health care is called:
questions.topic: Team concepts and community health care models

choices: Community paramedicine
Mobile integrated health care
Crew resource management
A mutual aid agreement
questions.explanation: Community paramedicine is the model in which experienced paramedics receive advanced training to provide added services like health evaluations, monitoring of chronic conditions, and patient advocacy.
questions.question: A service gives its experienced paramedics advanced additional training so they can perform health evaluations in patients' homes, monitor chronic illnesses between doctor visits, and advocate for their patients. This health care model is:
questions.topic: Team concepts and community health care models

choices: Continuum of care
Situational awareness
Mobile integrated health care
Crew resource management
questions.explanation: Crew resource management is a set of procedures for high-consequence environments that empowers team members to communicate effectively, improving situational awareness, patient and crew safety, and overall communication.
questions.question: Your service adopts a set of procedures borrowed from fields where a single human error can be disastrous. Under it, anyone on the crew is empowered to speak up, communication is structured, and the whole team works to maintain shared awareness of the situation. This system is called:
questions.topic: Team concepts and community health care models

choices: Crew resource management
Situational awareness
Continuum of care
Team leadership
questions.explanation: Situational awareness is knowledge and understanding of one's surroundings and the ability to recognize potential risks to the safety of the patient or the EMS team.
questions.question: A good provider constantly reads what's around the patient — noticing the crowd edging closer, the only exit getting blocked, and the unstable equipment near the patient's head — and recognizes the risks before anyone gets hurt. This knowledge and understanding of your surroundings is called:
questions.topic: Team concepts and community health care models

choices: A group, rather than a team
A continuum of care
A team, rather than a group
A mutual aid response
questions.explanation: A team is a set of providers assigned specific roles, working interdependently in a coordinated manner under a designated leader. Providers working independently are just a group.
questions.question: Two crews work the same kind of call. On the first, each provider picks his own task, nobody shares a plan, and there's no designated leader. On the second, providers hold assigned roles, work interdependently in a coordinated manner, and follow a designated leader. The second crew is best described as:
questions.topic: Team concepts and community health care models
